old: Its name traces to a verb meaning simply "to lift or raise" — nothing to do with blood at all, originally.
The Greek word it comes from once described the arteries branching straight out of the heart.
The lengthened Greek form aortéō, built on aeírō, gave English its word for the body's main artery.
clues: This blood vessel's name traces back to an ancient Greek verb meaning to lift or raise, an image of hoisting rather than flowing.
It is the body's largest artery, the main trunk rather than a branch, carrying oxygen-rich blood out of the heart's left ventricle. In Greek its name covered the arteries springing from the heart.
It arches over the top of the heart, then runs down through the chest and belly, and doctors watch it closely for dangerous bulges called aneurysms.
reviewNote: Clue 2's 'English borrowed its Greek name directly, meaning intact' was filler and read as if the name meant 'intact'; swapped for the entry's Greek-sense fact.
